title: Stopping antidepressants: withdrawal symptoms
blurb: Recognise antidepressant withdrawal, tell it apart from relapse and support a gradual, person-led taper.
question: Fatima, 37, stopped her venlafaxine abruptly 3 days ago because she felt better. She now has dizziness, 'electric shock' feelings in her head, irritability and poor sleep, and fears her depression is back. What is the best response?

teach.body: Antidepressant withdrawal symptoms are physical and emotional symptoms that can follow stopping abruptly, missing doses, not taking a full dose or reducing the dose. They can happen with TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and MAOIs. NICE says withdrawal does not affect everyone and varies in type and severity. In plain English: the brain has adapted to the drug, and taking it away too quickly causes temporary symptoms. It is not addiction and it is not the depression returning.

head: Area
Examples (NG222 1.4.13)
rows: Irritability, anxiety, low mood, panic, rarely suicidal thoughts

items.label: Symptoms may start after stopping or reducing

teach.caption: Severe withdrawal is more likely if the drug is stopped suddenly (NG222 1.4.14).
NG222 1.4.19: reassure people with withdrawal symptoms that they are not having a relapse.

teach.body: Paroxetine and venlafaxine are more likely to cause withdrawal symptoms, so particular care is needed; drugs with a short half-life are tapered more slowly. Fluoxetine lasts a long time in the body: at 20 mg a day, a period of alternate-day dosing can be enough; higher doses (40-60 mg) need a gradual schedule.

steps.label: Agree the plan
steps.sub: Led by and agreed with the person

steps.label: Reduce by a proportion
steps.sub: For example 50% of the previous dose

steps.label: Wait 1-2 weeks
steps.sub: Check symptoms are gone or tolerable

children.label: Monitor and reassure
children.sub: Common, usually time-limited; contact prescriber if worse

children.label: Consider restarting
children.sub: Previous dose, then slower taper with smaller steps

teach.body: Her community nurse explains that stopping venlafaxine suddenly commonly causes withdrawal; symptoms within days, with dizziness and shock sensations, fit withdrawal rather than relapse. Because they are distressing, he arranges a prompt review with her prescriber, who may restart the previous dose and plan a slower taper with smaller steps. He tells her that symptoms may take a few days to settle even after restarting, and agrees check-in calls.

teach.text: Do not label withdrawal as relapse and restart long-term treatment on that basis, and do not tell people withdrawal is always mild and brief. Current NICE advice (NG222 1.4.14) is that it is usually short, but can be severe and last weeks or occasionally months.

items: Abrupt stopping, missed doses or dose reductions can cause withdrawal.
Symptoms usually start within days and settle in 1-2 weeks, but can be severe or prolonged.
Paroxetine and venlafaxine carry higher risk; short half-life drugs need slower tapers.
Taper in proportional steps (e.g. 50%, then 25%), 1-2 weeks apart, agreed with the person.
Withdrawal is not relapse; if severe, restart the previous dose and taper more slowly.

summary: You can now recognise antidepressant withdrawal and explain how it differs from relapse. You can support a gradual, person-led taper and know what to do when symptoms are mild or severe.

A.q: According to NICE NG222, when do antidepressant withdrawal symptoms usually begin?
options: Within a few days of reducing or stopping
About 6 weeks after stopping
After the final dose has been fully stopped
After about 3 months off the drug
A.why: NG222 1.4.14: symptoms may appear within a few days of reducing or stopping and usually go within 1 to 2 weeks.

whyNot.1: Withdrawal typically starts within days, not weeks.
whyNot.2: Dose reductions and missed doses can also trigger withdrawal.
whyNot.3: Three months is far later than the usual onset.

A.q: Which two antidepressants does NICE name as more likely to cause withdrawal symptoms?
options: Fluoxetine and sertraline
Paroxetine and venlafaxine
Mirtazapine and citalopram
Fluoxetine and duloxetine
A.why: NG222 1.4.18: paroxetine and venlafaxine are more likely to be associated with withdrawal symptoms.

whyNot.0: Fluoxetine's long action makes withdrawal less of a problem.
whyNot.2: These are not the two drugs NICE singles out.
whyNot.3: Fluoxetine has a long duration of action and is not named as higher risk.

A.q: How long should usually be allowed between antidepressant dose reductions?
options: 1 to 2 days
3 to 4 days
1 to 2 weeks
2 to 3 months
A.why: NG222 1.4.18: allow 1 to 2 weeks to evaluate the effects of a dose reduction before the next.

whyNot.0: One to two days is too short to judge withdrawal effects.
whyNot.1: Three to four days is shorter than NICE advises.
whyNot.3: Two to three months between every step is longer than NICE suggests.

B.q: Rob, 45, is tapering sertraline. Five days after the latest reduction he feels dizzy and irritable and asks if his depression is coming back. What should the nurse say?
options: It is likely to be relapse and needs a higher dose
He should stop the remaining dose to finish quickly
It shows sertraline has stopped working for him
These are common withdrawal symptoms, not relapse
B.why: NG222 1.4.19: reassure people that withdrawal symptoms are not a relapse; relapse does not usually happen as soon as the dose is lowered.

whyNot.0: Timing and symptoms fit withdrawal; raising the dose long term is not indicated.
whyNot.1: Stopping abruptly increases the risk of severe withdrawal.
whyNot.2: Dizziness and irritability within days of a reduction fit withdrawal, not loss of the drug's effect.

B.q: Mia, 29, takes fluoxetine 20 mg daily and wants to stop. What does NICE say may be a suitable way to reduce?
options: Stop at once with no taper needed
Reduce by 10% every 6 weeks
A period of alternate-day dosing
Switch to paroxetine and then taper
B.why: NG222 1.4.18: because of fluoxetine's long action, a period of alternate-day dosing can provide a suitable reduction at 20 mg a day.

whyNot.0: NICE suggests a reduction step rather than no taper.
whyNot.1: This is slower than NICE suggests for fluoxetine 20 mg.
whyNot.3: Paroxetine is more likely to cause withdrawal, so switching to it makes no sense.

B.q: During a venlafaxine taper, Ade has severe dizziness, nausea and shock sensations that stop him working. What does NICE advise the prescriber to consider?
options: Continue the same schedule and add an antiemetic drug
Stop the drug completely to shorten symptoms
Switch to a different SNRI at a high dose
Restart the previous dose, then taper more slowly
B.why: NG222 1.4.21: with more severe withdrawal, consider restarting the original antidepressant at the previous dose, then reduce more slowly with smaller decrements once symptoms resolve.

whyNot.0: Pressing on with the same schedule ignores severe withdrawal.
whyNot.1: Stopping abruptly would make withdrawal worse.
whyNot.2: A high-dose switch is not the NICE approach to severe withdrawal.

C.q: Linda, 60, has taken paroxetine 40 mg for 8 years and is well. She wants to stop but fears withdrawal after a failed attempt last year. Which plan best follows NICE?
options: Halve to 20 mg, then stop completely 1 week later
Agree proportional steps that shrink as dose falls
Stop at once and treat any symptoms as they occur
Reduce by 10 mg every 3 days until stopped
C.why: NG222 1.4.15-1.4.16: offer extra support after previous difficulty; reduce step-wise by a proportion of the previous dose, using smaller reductions as the dose gets lower, at a pace led by the person.

whyNot.0: Going from 20 mg to zero in one step is too large a drop for paroxetine.
whyNot.2: Abrupt stopping makes severe withdrawal more likely.
whyNot.3: Three-day intervals are shorter than the 1 to 2 weeks NICE suggests.

C.q: Joe, 33, keeps forgetting doses of venlafaxine. Each time he misses one he feels dizzy and anxious the next day. What is the most helpful explanation?
options: Missed doses can trigger withdrawal
His depression returns when levels dip
He has become addicted to venlafaxine
His dose is too low and needs increasing
C.why: NG222 1.4.13: missing doses or not taking a full dose can cause withdrawal symptoms, and venlafaxine is more likely to do so. Adherence support helps.

whyNot.1: Rapid symptoms after one missed dose fit withdrawal, not relapse.
whyNot.2: Withdrawal symptoms do not mean addiction.
whyNot.3: The problem is missed doses, not an inadequate dose.

C.q: Bella, 26, restarted her previous citalopram dose yesterday because of severe withdrawal. She is upset that she still feels dizzy. What should the nurse explain?
options: The dose must be doubled to stop the dizziness
Persisting dizziness proves this is relapse
It may take a few days for symptoms to go
Citalopram should be stopped again at once
C.why: NG222 1.4.19: even after restarting or increasing the dose, withdrawal symptoms may take a few days to disappear.

whyNot.0: Doubling is not needed; symptoms usually ease within days.
whyNot.1: Continuing symptoms a day after restarting do not mean relapse.
whyNot.3: Stopping again would restart the withdrawal.

reteach.title: Slow down, don't stop
reteach.question: How do you help someone come off an antidepressant safely?

blocks.body: Plan the taper with the person. Reduce by a proportion of the current dose, wait 1 to 2 weeks, and go smaller as the dose falls. Symptoms within days of a change are usually withdrawal, not relapse. If they are severe, go back to the last dose and go slower.

blocks.caption: Illustration of proportional steps only; the actual schedule is set by the prescriber with the person.

blocks.text: Withdrawal symptoms are not relapse and not addiction.

explain.body: Stopping abruptly, missing doses, not taking a full dose or reducing the dose can all cause withdrawal. It can occur with TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and MAOIs.

test.q: Which antidepressant classes can cause withdrawal symptoms?
options: SSRIs and SNRIs, but not TCAs
TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and MAOIs
MAOIs and TCAs, but not SSRIs
SNRIs, but not SSRIs or TCAs
test.why: NG222 1.4.18: withdrawal symptoms can occur with a wide range of antidepressants, including TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and MAOIs.

whyNot.3: SSRIs and TCAs can also cause withdrawal.

explain.body: Usually mild, starting within a few days and settling within 1 to 2 weeks. Sometimes more difficult, lasting several weeks or occasionally months, and can be severe if stopped suddenly.

test.q: What should people be told about how long withdrawal symptoms last?
options: They usually stop within 24 hours
They usually last at least 6 months
They last for the length of treatment
Usually 1-2 weeks, sometimes longer
test.why: NG222 1.4.14: symptoms usually go within 1 to 2 weeks but can last several weeks and occasionally several months.

whyNot.0: Symptoms commonly last longer than a day.
whyNot.1: Most people's symptoms settle much sooner than 6 months.
whyNot.2: Duration is not matched to time on treatment.

explain.body: Reduce step-wise, prescribing a proportion of the previous dose (e.g. 50%), with smaller reductions (e.g. 25%) as the dose falls; liquid forms can help at low doses. Allow 1 to 2 weeks between steps. The person leads the pace.

test.q: As the dose gets lower during a taper, what does NICE suggest?
options: Larger reductions to finish sooner
Stopping once half the dose is reached
Smaller reductions, such as 25%
Daily reductions to limit symptoms
test.why: NG222 1.4.16: consider smaller reductions (for example 25%) as the dose becomes lower, and liquid preparations if needed.

whyNot.0: Larger steps at low doses tend to cause more withdrawal.
whyNot.1: Stopping at half dose is an abrupt drop.
whyNot.3: Daily changes do not allow 1 to 2 weeks to assess each step.

explain.body: Mild: monitor, reassure that symptoms are common and time-limited, and contact the prescriber if they worsen. Severe: consider restarting the previous dose and then tapering more slowly with smaller steps.

test.q: Eve has mild dizziness 4 days after a dose reduction. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Monitor and reassure that it is common
Restart the full original dose today
Stop the antidepressant completely now
Refer urgently to the local crisis team
test.why: NG222 1.4.20: for mild symptoms, monitor, reassure that they are common and usually time-limited, and advise contacting the prescriber if they persist or worsen.

whyNot.1: Restarting is considered for severe symptoms.
whyNot.3: Mild withdrawal does not need a crisis response.
